spans.s:
maṭha
(‘dwelling place of yatis or मोन्क्स्’)
------------------------------------------
A मठ (monastery), in the sense we understand it today, is, perhaps, not a very ancient institution. The Baudhāyana Dharmasūtras (

) (600-300 B. C.) has used the word ‘maṭha’ in the sense of a hut where a teacher and his pupils reside, to pursue their studies. Maṭhas might have evolved from the example of the Buddhist vihāras. They definitely received a fillip from the celebrated teacher of Advaita Vedānta, शङ्कर (A.

-820), who established four principal maṭhas in the four cardinal directions of India.
A temple and a मठ both have a common religious motive and sentiment. However, if a temple is built primarily for the purpose of prayer and worship as also religious instruction for the masses in a general way, a मठ is specially meant for the training of the pupils and the laity in the tenets of the sect to which it belongs or in the doctrines of some philosophy including allied fields of knowledge. The heads of these maṭhas were, generally, saṁnyāsins (monks) and were called ‘maṭhādhipatis’ (‘mahanta’ in vernaculars).
Originally the maṭhas were simple dwelling places for these मोन्क्स् since they were expected to constantly tour the country for spreading the message of धर्म (moral and spiritual values). However, due to the enthusiasm and generosity of the laity, these maṭhas gradually acquired a lot of property, both movable and immovable. This naturally necessitated the evolution of some norms, guidelines and rules for the judicious management of the मठ and its property. Related to it was also the problem of succession.
Though the entire property belonged to the मठ, its legal head (the maṭhādhipati) had the full control and the freedom to use it in the best interests of the institution and its followers.
A maṭhādhipati is selected in one of the three ways as follows:
The present head selects from among his disciples a fit one to succeed him.
The disciples will elect from among themselves one person if the previous head had passed away without choosing his successor.
The ruling power (the State) or the original founder or his heirs appoint the next head.
Over the centuries, maṭhas of various sects have proliferated.
As the properties and income of these maṭhas went on swelling, disputes over their control as also the rights and privileges, also increased. Consequently law-courts have been flooded with cases related to these disputes.
However, whenever a spiritually eminent person has occupied the pontiff’s seat, really great work has been done for the welfare of Hindu society by these maṭhas. Types of service also have been increased and diversified.
Wherever an important temple and a मठ have been closely associated with each other, both have grown in quantity and quality.
